result: The study presents a 3.3 Å resolution cryo-EM structure of the open conformation of Drosophila Orai H206A mutant using fiducial-assisted cryo-electron microscopy with Fab antibody fragments. The structure reveals conformations of amino acids in the open pore with the central region (M1, M2, M3 helices and Fab variable domains) resolved at ~3.1 Å resolution, while peripheral regions (M4 helices and Fab constant domains) are less well defined.
evaluation: Claims C6, C65-68, C81, and C84 collectively demonstrate successful structure determination at 3.3 Å resolution using cryo-EM with Fab fiducials. The resolution estimates are based on gold-standard FSC calculations (C65), local resolution analysis shows differential quality across regions (C66-67), and the structure agrees with previous low-resolution X-ray data (C81). The atomic model content is clearly defined (C68), and side chain conformations are resolved for most pore-lining residues (C84).

result: The monoclonal antibody 19B5 was developed as a fiducial marker that binds to the M1-M2 loop on the extracellular side of Orai without affecting Ca2+ influx. Cryo-EM analysis revealed Orai-Fab complexes with 1-3 Fabs per hexameric channel, with the 3-Fab complexes yielding the highest resolution maps and displaying C3 symmetry.
evaluation: Claims C55-79 and C209 provide comprehensive evidence for antibody development and characterization. The antibody was raised against native Orai (C55), binds to the M1-M2 loop (C56), does not affect channel function (C57), and binds in cellular context (C58). Cryo-EM analysis shows variable Fab stoichiometry (C59-61), extracellular epitope location (C62), and that 3-Fab complexes yield highest resolution (C63-64). Structural analysis confirms binding adjacent to pore entrance (C70-74, C77-79) without functional inhibition (C73). This demonstrates successful application of Fab fiducials for small protein structure determination (C209).

result: The open pore structure reveals that channel opening occurs through rigid-body outward movements of subunits (~2.5 Å at Phe 171) without significant helical rotation or side chain conformational changes. A ring of phenylalanine residues (Phe 171) repositions through outward sliding to expose previously shielded glycine residues (Gly 170) to the pore, widening the pore along its entire length.
evaluation: Claims C7-9, C85-86, C109-110, C112-113, C117-120, C129-131, C139, C141-143 collectively demonstrate the gating mechanism. The structure shows outward subunit movements (C8, C120, C129-131) with specific measurements (~2.5 Å at Phe 171, C113, C130). Phe 171 repositions without helical rotation (C9, C117, C119) to expose Gly 170 (C117, C146). The mechanism differs from other ion channels (C141) and involves rigid-body motions without side chain rearrangements (C139, C142-143). Dilation occurs throughout the pore (C86, C110, C196-198).

result: The structure reveals structured M1-M2 turrets (amino acids 179-189) that form the extracellular entrance of the pore, extending ~20 Å above the selectivity filter with an inverted V-shape. The turrets contain a conserved VQLD motif and create a funnel-shaped entrance (~20 Å diameter) with a markedly negative electrostatic surface that would concentrate cations near the pore entrance.
evaluation: Claims C11-12, C75-76, C80, C82, C87-97, C154-155 provide comprehensive structural and functional characterization of the M1-M2 turrets. The turrets were not evident in previous structures (C12, C80) but are clearly resolved in the cryo-EM structure (C75-76, C87-89). Structural details include the VQLD motif (C92-94), hydrophobic stabilization network (C94), and hydrogen bonding to M3 (C90-91). The funnel-shaped entrance (C95) with negative electrostatic surface (C96-97, C154-155) provides a structural basis for cation concentration, supported by previous functional studies (C155).

result: The glutamate ring (Glu 178) forms the selectivity filter and is the narrowest constriction of the open pore. The cryo-EM structure shows Ca2+ density at the center of the ring, with weak density suggesting Glu 178 side chains adopt alternating up-down rotamer conformations. The helical backbone shifts ~1 Å outward relative to the closed conformation, indicating dilation of the selectivity filter upon opening.
evaluation: Claims C98-110, C158-164 demonstrate selectivity filter structure and conformational changes. The glutamate ring is the narrowest constriction (C98) and forms the selectivity filter (C99). Ca2+ density is present (C100-101), consistent with previous Ba2+ binding studies (C101, C161-162). Weak density for Glu 178 side chains (C102) suggests alternating conformations (C103-104), though this may be influenced by C3 symmetry (C105). The backbone shifts ~1 Å outward (C109), indicating filter dilation (C110). Multiple lines of evidence support filter conformational changes (C158-163), distinguishing Orai from classical K+ channels (C164).

result: The hydrophobic region (Leu 167, Phe 171, Val 174) functions as the primary gate of the channel. In the closed state, Phe 171 residues are in close proximity near the pore axis (diameter 5-6 Å), stabilized by hydrophobic packing and van der Waals contacts with Gly 170. In the open state, the region widens to 9-10 Å through outward subunit movements, with Phe 171 sliding outward to expose Gly 170 to the pore.
evaluation: Claims C10, C53-54, C111-117, C144-148, C184-187, C193, C200, C204 establish the hydrophobic region as the primary gate. The region comprises conserved residues (C111) that are markedly wider in the open state (C112-113). Phe 171 positioning and interactions are well-defined in closed (C114-116) and open (C117) states. The structure agrees with cysteine accessibility experiments (C144-145) and molecular dynamics simulations (C147-148). The diameter measurements (5-6 Å closed, 9-10 Å open, C193) correspond to hydrophobic dewetting transitions (C191-192). The mechanism is simpler than other channels (C204) and represents a consensus view (C184, C200).

result: The pore contains a highly basic region comprising 18 conserved lysine/arginine residues (Arg 155, Lys 159, Lys 163) that is markedly wider in the open conformation (12 Å increase at Lys 159). The anion/iron complex present in the closed state is absent in the open structure. Multiple lines of evidence suggest the basic region does not form the primary gate but may be important for channel opening and Ca2+ permeation through anion shielding.
evaluation: Claims C121-128, C175-183 characterize the basic region structure and function. The region contains 18 conserved basic residues (C121-122) that form anion binding sites in the closed state (C123-124). The region widens significantly upon opening (C125, C175) and loses the anion plug (C126, C175). Basic residues are exposed to the pore (C127). Multiple functional studies show the basic region is not the primary gate: mutations to acidic residues still require STIM (C178), triple serine substitution doesn't create constitutive activity (C180) but prevents STIM activation (C181). The hypothesis of anion shielding (C128, C182) is supported by I- binding data (C183).

result: The H206A mutation, located on M2 helix and not exposed to the pore, eliminates a hydrogen bond with Ser 165 and diminishes van der Waals interactions, altering the free energy profile to favor the open state. A histidine can be readily modeled back into the structure, suggesting the wild-type channel can adopt this conformation when activated by STIM.
evaluation: Claims C132-138 explain the structural basis for H206A constitutive activity. The M4 bend changes in the open state (C132-133). His 206 is on M2, not the pore (C134), and forms specific interactions in wild-type (C135). The H206A mutation eliminates these interactions (C136), altering energetics to favor opening (C137). Modeling shows wild-type can adopt this conformation (C138), supported by previous studies showing H134A (human Orai1 equivalent) has similar properties to STIM-activated channels (C32-34).

result: The P288L mutation structures reported by Liu et al. likely represent a closed conformation rather than an open state. The hydrophobic region is narrow, density for an anion plug is present, and purified P288L Orai does not show ion permeation in liposomes, suggesting the mutation may require STIM for activation in cells.
evaluation: Claims C149-153 provide a reinterpretation of published P288L structures. The structural comparison shows the P288L conformation is similar to the unlatched-closed state (C150), with narrow hydrophobic region (C150) and anion plug density (C151). Functional data from the current study shows no ion permeation in liposomes (C152), contrasting with cell-based activation. The hypothesis that P288L requires endogenous STIM (C153) reconciles these observations, though this remains speculative and would require additional experiments to confirm.

result: The authors hypothesize a Ca2+ selectivity mechanism involving transient single-file positioning of two Ca2+ ions in the filter, with flexibility of Glu 178 side chains facilitating this accommodation. The filter typically contains one Ca2+ ion that blocks monovalent flux, with a second Ca2+ causing dissociation of the first through electrostatic repulsion.
evaluation: Claims C165-174 present a mechanistic hypothesis for Ca2+ selectivity. While the hypothesis is consistent with classical Ca2+ selectivity models (C165) and supported by concatemer experiments (C170-171), it remains speculative (evidence_type: SPECULATION for C165-169). The weak density for Glu 178 side chains (C102-103) and structural observations of alternating conformations (C103, C172) provide some support, but the resolution limitations prevent direct observation of the proposed mechanism. The hypothesis about M1 cytosolic region ordering by STIM (C174) is also speculative. Additional high-resolution structures and functional studies would be needed to validate this model.

result: Background knowledge about Orai channels: Orai regulates Ca2+ entry in non-excitable cells and is required for immune function. The channel typically opens following ER Ca2+ depletion, but certain pathologic mutations (including H206A/H134A) render it constitutively open. The H134A mutant exhibits properties similar to STIM-activated wild-type channels.
evaluation: Claims C1-38 establish the biological and experimental context. These are primarily established knowledge claims (evidence_type: KNOWLEDGE, CITATION) about Orai function (C1-2, C13-14), activation mechanism (C3, C15), disease associations (C27-28, C30), and gain-of-function mutations (C4, C29-38). The H206A mutation used in this study corresponds to H134A in human Orai1 (C32-35), which has been extensively characterized as producing an open conformation similar to STIM-activated channels (C32-34, C36-38). These claims provide essential context but are not novel findings of the current study.

result: Previous structural studies established that Orai is a hexameric channel with four transmembrane helices per subunit (M1-M4), where M1 helices form the ~55 Å long pore. The M1-M2 linkages were not clearly resolved in previous structures but were suggested to contribute to the extracellular entrance based on functional studies.
evaluation: Claims C39-54 summarize previous structural knowledge about Orai. The hexameric architecture (C39-42) and transmembrane topology (C43-48) are well-established from prior X-ray structures (evidence_type: CITATION, DATA). The limitations regarding M1-M2 linkage resolution (C49) and functional evidence for its role in pore entrance (C50-52) provide important context for the current study's resolution of the M1-M2 turrets. The hydrophobic gate hypothesis (C53-54) from previous studies is validated by the current structure. These claims establish the foundation for interpreting the new structural findings.

result: The structure provides a framework for understanding Orai function in the context of established principles: acidic residues in the entrance affect Gd3+ block but not Ca2+ selectivity; hydrophobic gating involves dewetting transitions at ~9 Å diameter; and different ion channels use diverse mechanisms for hydrophobic gate control, with Orai using rigid-body subunit movements controlled by STIM from the cytosolic side.
evaluation: Claims C156-157, C188-195, C200-208, C210 integrate the current structural findings with established principles and prior knowledge. Functional studies of entrance mutations (C156-157) are consistent with the structure. Hydrophobic gating principles from simulations (C188-195) align well with Orai's structural dimensions (C193). Comparisons with other channels (C200-203, C205-206) highlight Orai's unique mechanism (C204, C207). The statement that the mechanism for STIM-induced opening remains unresolved (C208) is accurate. The claim that this work provides a framework for future studies (C210) is supported by the comprehensive structural characterization.
